Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences

Son T. Huynh Email: htson@hcmus.edu.vn Affiliation: AISIA Research Lab, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Affiliation: Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Science, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Affiliation: Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam    Thuy T. Abstract

Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate’s genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment–contig–isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall for all three antibiotics when isolates are shared across splits, and smaller drug-dependent gains when test isolates are held out entirely. Gains concentrate in whichever class the baseline classifier handles worst.

keywords
Antimicrobial resistance, Genome-to-image translation, Conditional GAN, Genomic language model, Data augmentation, Escherichia coli

1 Introduction

Antimicrobial resistance limits the treatment options available for common bacterial infections, and Escherichia coli bloodstream infection is among the settings where the cost of an ineffective first-line choice is highest Murray et al. (2022); World Health Organization (2022). In routine practice the resistance profile of an isolate is established by culture-based antimicrobial susceptibility testing, which requires the organism to grow under each candidate drug before a phenotype can be read out. The resulting delay is incompatible with the clinical need to commit to a therapy early, so the initial prescription is frequently empirical and is revised once susceptibility results arrive van Belkum et al. (2020).

Two developments make it reasonable to ask whether this phenotype can be anticipated computationally. The first is that drug exposure and resistance status are visible in the cell itself: susceptible and resistant E. coli differ in subcellular morphology under antibiotic challenge strongly enough that a convolutional classifier can separate them from microscopy alone Zagajewski et al. (2023). The second is that whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates has become routine, and genomic language models pretrained on large nucleotide corpora now provide general-purpose representations of raw sequence without task-specific feature engineering Zhou et al. (2024). Taken together, these suggest that the genome of an isolate carries information about how that isolate will look under a given drug, not only about which resistance determinants it carries.

Existing work does not connect these two ends. Genotype-to-phenotype prediction has overwhelmingly treated the phenotype as a scalar or structured numerical target, including genome-based prediction of resistance itself Su et al. (2019), so the visual morphology of the organism is never modelled. Conditional image generation from molecular descriptors, meanwhile, has been developed for eukaryotic systems and is conditioned on processed readouts such as gene expression, chemical structure, or a discrete perturbation label Lee and Welch (2022); Yang et al. (2021); Palma et al. (2025); Navidi et al. (2024); Cai et al. (2026). The one method we are aware of that generates morphological images directly from DNA, G2PDiffusion Liu et al. (2025), targets morphological diversity across insect taxa using multiple sequence alignments and geographic metadata, and has no notion of drug treatment or resistance. To our knowledge, no prior method conditions image generation on an embedding learned from raw bacterial sequencing reads, nor relates the generated images to an antimicrobial resistance phenotype.

This paper addresses that gap. We cast the problem as genome-to-image translation for a single clinically relevant species and build a conditional generative framework with two parts. A genomic encoding pipeline takes the raw paired-end reads of an isolate through quality control, merging, assembly, and annotation, then encodes the resulting contigs into one fixed-length 768-dimensional vector with a frozen DNABERT-2 encoder, aggregating hierarchically from segments to contigs to the isolate with a length-aware weighted average. A conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP) Gulrajani et al. (2017) then synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and, in the second training phase, the resistance status of the isolate. The adversarial formulation with gradient penalty is chosen deliberately over a diffusion backbone: our dataset comprises a single species represented by 22 isolates, a regime in which a data-intensive generative model is difficult to justify.

The setting also shapes how we evaluate. Intrinsic generative metrics report whether synthetic images resemble real ones distributionally, but they do not establish that the images are biologically informative. We therefore pair FID, KID, and SSIM with a task-based benchmark: synthetic cells conditioned on antibiotic and resistance status are added to a deliberately reduced real training set, and we measure what they do to a downstream per-antibiotic resistance classifier across five seeds with paired significance testing, under both a permissive split and a stricter split in which no test isolate is seen during training.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We formulate bacterial genome-to-image translation conditioned on a genomic foundation-model embedding, the applied antibiotic, and the resistance phenotype, which to our knowledge has not been attempted for bacterial morphology or antimicrobial resistance.

  • •

    We describe a reproducible genomic encoding pipeline that maps raw paired-end reads to a single isolate-level embedding, including an adaptive read-merging threshold derived per isolate from the observed insert-size distribution rather than a fixed cutoff.

  • •

    We report a controlled ablation of seven ImageNet-pretrained CNN backbones inside the generator under identical training conditions, and document two concrete training failure modes of the naive formulation together with the objective design that resolves them.

  • •

    We evaluate the synthetic images extrinsically rather than only intrinsically, showing that GAN augmentation improves resistant-class recall under a low-data regime and that the gains concentrate in the class the baseline classifier handles worst, while being explicit about the accompanying precision trade-off and about the limits of training the generator and the classifier on the same dataset.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews molecularly conditioned image generation and morphology-based resistance characterization. Section 3 describes the paired sequencing and imaging data and the splitting protocols. Section 4 presents the genomic encoding pipeline and the cWGAN-GP framework. Section 5 reports the backbone ablation and the downstream classification results, and Section 6 concludes.

2 Related Work

The most closely related line of work generates cellular images from molecular descriptors, motivated largely by phenotypic drug discovery and high-content microscopy. We review it in detail because it shares our core setting, in which a generator is conditioned on a molecular representation to synthesize a morphological image.

An early instance is MorphNet Lee and Welch (2022), which learns the conditional distribution of cell morphology given single-cell gene expression by pairing a variational autoencoder that compresses the expression vector with a generative adversarial network that decodes the resulting representation into an image. Mol2Image Yang et al. (2021) instead conditions a flow-based generative model on the chemical structure of a compound, synthesizing cell microscopy images for unseen molecular interventions through a multi-scale architecture trained with a contrastive objective. More recent methods scale this idea and improve generalization. IMPA Palma et al. (2025) casts perturbation prediction as a style-transfer problem, using an autoencoder-based conditional adversarial model to predict how a control cell would appear under a given chemical or genetic intervention, and demonstrates extrapolation to perturbations not seen during training on breast cancer and osteosarcoma cell lines. MorphoDiff Navidi et al. (2024) integrates perturbation embeddings as guiding signals within a latent diffusion model and produces high-resolution morphological predictions that generalize across both chemical and genetic interventions on Cell Painting datasets. A parallel thread targets histopathology, where the molecular signal is gene expression and the image is a tissue section. GE2Hist Cai et al. (2026) derives cell-state representations from single-cell gene expression using a single-cell foundation model and conditions a diffusion model to synthesize histological images that reconstruct cellular composition and spatial organization. Related efforts extend this multimodal coupling to jointly predict morphology and expression and to adapt pretrained diffusion models to data-limited institutional settings, reflecting growing interest in molecularly conditioned image synthesis for tissue.

Two observations follow from this body of work, and together they motivate the present study. First, the molecular conditioning signal in all of these methods is a processed, eukaryotic readout, namely gene expression, chemical structure, or a discrete perturbation label, rather than a representation derived directly from raw genomic sequence. Second, the biological targets are exclusively eukaryotic, comprising cultured mammalian cell lines and human tissue sections, with no treatment of bacterial morphology or the clinical question of antimicrobial resistance. To our knowledge, no prior method conditions image generation on an embedding learned directly from raw bacterial sequencing reads, nor links the generated images to antimicrobial resistance phenotypes, which is precisely the gap this work addresses.

Predicting phenotype from genotype is a long-standing problem, but most computational approaches predict scalar or structured numerical traits rather than images, treating the phenotype as a low-dimensional regression or classification target and therefore never modelling the visual morphology of the organism. Recasting genotype-to-phenotype prediction as image generation is recent, and to the best of our knowledge G2PDiffusion Liu et al. (2025) is the only existing method that generates morphological images directly from genomic sequence. It treats images as morphological proxies and conditions a diffusion model on a genotype-environment representation built from two evolutionary signals: a multiple sequence alignment (MSA), retrieved from an external database with MMseqs2 to capture conserved and co-evolutionary regions, and geographic coordinates encoding environmental context. Trained on the BIOSCAN-5M dataset of over five million insect specimens paired with DNA barcodes, coordinates, and images, it is evaluated against adapted conditional generation baselines using alignment- and embedding-based measures of genotype-phenotype consistency.

Although G2PDiffusion and our work share the high-level idea of generating images from DNA, they differ in ways that matter for the antimicrobial resistance setting. G2PDiffusion studies morphological diversity across diverse insect taxa and has no notion of drug treatment or resistance, whereas our generator targets a single clinically relevant species, E. coli, and is conditioned on the applied antibiotic and a binary resistance label so that the synthesized colony morphology reflects a specific drug exposure and resistance state. Their conditioning signal is an MSA assembled by cross-species homology retrieval augmented with geographic metadata, whereas ours is a fixed-length isolate-level embedding produced directly by a genomic foundation model from each isolate’s assembled reads, requiring neither homology retrieval nor environmental coordinates. The two settings also occupy opposite data regimes: G2PDiffusion is a diffusion model trained on more than five million DNA-image pairs, while our setting comprises a single species represented by only 22 isolates, a scarcity that partly motivates our choice of an adversarial objective with gradient penalty over a data-intensive diffusion backbone. Finally, G2PDiffusion is evaluated intrinsically, through DNA-image alignment and phenotype embedding similarity, whereas our central evaluation is extrinsic: synthetic images augment a downstream resistance classifier whose per-antibiotic performance is assessed with explicit significance testing. To our knowledge, no prior genome-to-image method addresses bacterial morphology or antimicrobial resistance, which is the gap this work targets.

A separate line of work establishes that antimicrobial susceptibility leaves a visible morphological signature in bacterial cells, and exploits this signal discriminatively. Most directly related is DASP Zagajewski et al. (2023), which images fluorescently stained E. coli cells and trains convolutional networks to classify individual cells as susceptible or resistant from subcellular morphology, across four antibiotics with distinct mechanisms of action including ciprofloxacin, and validates the approach on clinical isolates. This confirms the premise underlying our work, namely that resistance status is encoded in cellular appearance, but it is a purely discriminative method: it classifies existing images rather than generating them, and it is conditioned on the image alone, with no genomic input. Generative models have separately been applied to bacterial imaging, but not for resistance characterization. Specifically, CycleGAN-based translation has been used to turn procedurally generated colony images into realistic microscopy for training segmentation models Hickl et al. (2025), and related efforts synthesize bacterial or biofilm imagery to enlarge training sets or emulate staining. In all of these cases the generator is conditioned on image-derived or procedural signals rather than on genomic information, and none addresses antimicrobial resistance. Our work differs from both threads: rather than classifying images discriminatively or generating images from image-derived cues, we generate resistance-conditioned colony images from a genomic embedding and use them to improve a downstream resistance classifier. In doing so, this work contributes an application of conditional generative modeling to a biological imaging domain, extending GenAI-based synthesis beyond the natural-image and human-communication settings in which it is most often studied toward the simulation of microbiological systems from molecular descriptors. It also contributes on the evaluation axis: beyond reporting standard intrinsic generative metrics (FID, KID, SSIM), we adopt a task-based benchmark in which the synthesized images are assessed by their measurable utility for a downstream resistance-classification task, with per-antibiotic performance quantified across multiple seeds under explicit significance testing. This pairing of intrinsic image-quality metrics with an extrinsic, task-grounded benchmark speaks directly to the need for rigorous evaluation protocols for generative models in applied, high-stakes domains.

3 Dataset

3.1 Data Acquisition

This study pairs two modalities acquired from the same collection of bacterial isolates: whole-genome sequencing of each isolate, and colony microscopy of that isolate imaged under an antibiotic panel. Both modalities are keyed by isolate identifier, which is what allows a genomic representation to be used as the conditioning signal for an image of the same organism.

Isolates and sequencing.

The genomic material originates from the 19EN_single_isolate_fromBlood collection, comprising 27 single-isolate samples recovered from blood specimens and used here for species identification and for genomic encoding. Each isolate was sequenced under a paired-end protocol, and the reads of an isolate were archived as two gzip-compressed FASTQ files corresponding to the forward and reverse mates (R1.fastq.gz and R2.fastq.gz). Read quality, adapter content, and insert-size distribution were assessed per isolate as part of the preprocessing pipeline described in Section 4.1; no isolate was excluded on the basis of sequencing quality.

Imaging.

Colony microscopy was performed in three sessions on three separate dates, yielding the three imaging disks summarized in Table 1, with nine isolates imaged per disk. On every disk each isolate was imaged under the full panel of four conditions: azithromycin (AZI), ciprofloxacin (CIP), tetracycline (TE), and an untreated no-drug control, so that the morphological effect of a drug can be read against the untreated appearance of the same isolate. The ATCC 25922 reference strain of E. coli was imaged alongside the clinical isolates as a quality control for the imaging protocol; because no sequencing data exist for it, it carries no genomic embedding and is excluded from all modelling. Acquisition produced 549 microscopy images in total, from which 173,081 individual cell images were obtained by segmenting and cropping each detected cell to its own image. All experiments in this paper operate on these single-cell crops rather than on whole microscopy fields.

Resistance labelling.

Every isolate–antibiotic pair carries a binary ground-truth phenotype, resistant (R) or susceptible (S), determined by antimicrobial susceptibility testing independently of the imaging. These labels are the targets of the downstream classification task in Section 5.2 and the resistance conditioning signal of the Phase 2 generator. Labels are defined only for the three antibiotic-treated conditions; no-drug control images carry no resistance label and are therefore excluded wherever the resistance phenotype is required.

3.2 Data Overview

The dataset used in this study consists of two complementary data modalities: whole-genome sequencing data and microscopy image data, both derived from bacterial isolates.

3.2.1 Genome Sequencing data

We use genome sequencing from the 19EN_single_isolate_fromBlood dataset, comprising 27 isolates collected from blood samples, for species identification. For each isolate, paired-end reads were stored as R1/R2 FASTQ files (R1/R2.fastq.gz).

3.2.2 Image data

Colony microscopy images are collected across three imaging sessions conducted on three separate dates: disk 1 (22/12/2021), disk 2 (30/12/2021), and disk 3 (01/01/2022); each disk covers a distinct set of nine isolates. On each disk, every isolate is imaged under a full antibiotic panel comprising four treatment conditions: azithromycin (AZI), ciprofloxacin (CIP), tetracycline (TE), and a no-drug control. The per-disk statistics are summarized in Table 1.

Among the 549 images, 29 images (5,725 cells) correspond to the ATCC 25922 reference strain, which lacks genomic sequence data and is therefore excluded from downstream analysis. The remaining 520 images (167,356 cells) represent 22 unique clinical isolates, all of blood origin, which constitute the working dataset for this study.

3.2.3 Data splitting

To accommodate the distinct objectives and metadata criteria of each research phase, the data partitioning strategy for training, validation, and testing sets varies across phases, as detailed below.

Phase 1 (cWGAN-GP)

For the generative modeling phase, the dataset was partitioned at the single-cell level into training, validation, and testing sets with a 70:20:10 ratio. Cell-level splitting is adopted because several isolate–antibiotic combinations contain only a single image, making image-level partitioning infeasible for meaningful evaluation. To preserve experimental diversity, each split is stratified to ensure all 22 isolates and all four treatment conditions are represented, and the 70:20:10 ratio is enforced within every isolate–antibiotic subgroup. The resulting partition yields 117,106 cells for training, 33,473 for validation, and 16,777 for testing (total: 167,356 cells).

Phase 2 (AMR classification)

For the downstream resistance/susceptibility classification task, two data-partitioning strategies were considered, both performed at the image level into training, validation, and testing sets to prevent data leakage. Since a single microscopy image can contain hundreds of individual bacterial cell images, these cell images may share the same resistance/susceptibility label, which would undermine the reliability of evaluation on the test set if they were scattered randomly across different splits. Accordingly, all cell images originating from the same microscopy image are assigned exclusively to a single data split. Only images from the three antibiotic-treated conditions (AZI, CIP, TE) are included; no-drug control images are excluded as they carry no resistance or susceptibility label and are therefore not applicable to the binary classification objective. The per-antibiotic split statistics for the two strategies are reported in Tables 2 and 3.

Isolate-agnostic splitting. In the first strategy, isolate identity is not taken into account: microscopy images from all isolates are pooled and randomly partitioned into training, validation, and testing sets at the image level. As a result, images from the same isolate may appear in different splits, although cell images from the same microscopy image are still never separated. This setting is less stringent and measures performance when the model has already encountered the isolates during training.

Isolate-aware splitting. In the second strategy, the training and testing sets are separated at the isolate level, so that no isolate appears in both sets. Specifically, ∼\sim80% of the isolates are assigned to the training set and the remaining isolates form the testing set. The validation set is then drawn from the training set, accounting for ∼\sim25% of its microscopy images, and is split at the image level. Consequently, an isolate belonging to the training portion may contribute images to both the training and validation sets, but never to the testing set. This strategy evaluates the model’s ability to generalize to previously unseen isolates, which more closely reflects real-world deployment.

Under both strategies, the class distribution across splits for all three antibiotics is moderately imbalanced, with resistant images accounting for approximately 50% to 76% of each split, reflecting the clinical prevalence of resistance among the collected isolates.

4 Methodology

We propose a conditional generative framework that synthesizes colony microscopy images of bacterial isolates from genomic and phenotypic information. Figure 1 provides an overview of the complete system.

The framework comprises two components. The first is a genomic encoding pipeline that transforms raw paired-end sequencing reads into a fixed-length 768-dimensional isolate embedding using DNABERT-2, a transformer pretrained on large-scale genomic corpora. This embedding serves as the primary conditioning signal throughout the generative model, encoding the genomic identity of the isolate in a form that the GAN can consume directly. The second is a conditional Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (cWGAN-GP) which generates synthetic colony images from the isolate embedding, an antibiotic treatment label, and a sampled latent noise vector, described in detail in Section 4.2. The GAN is conditioned on all available biological context so that the generated images reflect the combined effect of genomic background, drug exposure, and resistance phenotype.

The GAN framework is developed across two training phases, each serving a distinct purpose. Phase 1 is a backbone ablation study: seven pretrained CNN architectures are evaluated as the visual feature extractor inside the generator under identical training conditions, with the model conditioned on the isolate embedding and the antibiotic label. The best-performing backbone is selected based on FID, KID, and SSIM computed on the test set. Phase 2 builds on Phase 1 by training the selected model (ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone Liu et al. (2022)) with an additional condition: the antimicrobial resistance status of the isolate. This extension enables the model to generate images that distinguish between resistant and sensitive phenotypes under each antibiotic, directly supporting the downstream resistance classification task described in Section 5.2.

4.1 Genomic Sequence Encoding

The complete genomic encoding pipeline is illustrated in Figure 2. It consists of two stages: a sequence preprocessing stage that converts raw sequencing reads into clean, annotated contigs, and a sequence encoding stage that maps those contigs into a single fixed-length vector per isolate.

Sequence Preprocessing

Raw paired-end sequencing reads in FASTQ format are processed through a five-stage preprocessing pipeline whose goal is to remove low-quality data and reconstruct, for each isolate, a clean set of annotated genomic contigs. Each pair of FASTQ files is first inspected with FastQC Andrews et al. (2017), which reports per-base quality scores, GC content distribution, sequence duplication levels, and potential adapter contamination. Based on this assessment, the reads are cleaned with FASTP Chen et al. (2018): adapter sequences are detected automatically in paired-end mode, and bases with a Phred quality score below 20 (an estimated error probability above 1%1\%) are trimmed. The cleaned forward and reverse reads of each pair are then merged into single contiguous reads using VSEARCH Rognes et al. (2016). Rather than employing a fixed threshold, the minimum overlap length required for the merging process is dynamically determined for each isolate based on the insert size distribution mean extracted from the FASTP post-filtering metadata. The algorithm allows at most five mismatches within this overlap region, and merged reads falling below the calculated adaptive threshold are discarded to eliminate spuriously short products. For each isolate, the merged reads are assembled into genomic contigs using SPAdes Bankevich et al. (2012) in careful mode, which enables an additional post-assembly step that corrects mismatches and short indels. Finally, the assembled contigs are annotated with Bakta Schwengers et al. (2021) using its lightweight database, producing sequences in .fna format and standardizing contig identifiers and sequence representation across all 22 isolates for consistent input to the encoding stage.

Sequence Encoding with DNABERT-2

To represent each isolate as a dense vector, we use DNABERT-2 Zhou et al. (2024) as a frozen feature extractor, which lets us reuse its pretrained genomic representations while avoiding the computational cost of fine-tuning. Encoding proceeds through a hierarchy of three levels: segment, contig, and isolate. Because transformer encoders accept only a limited input length, each contig is first split into overlapping segments of 512 bp using a sliding window with a stride of 256 bp, where the 256 bp overlap between adjacent windows preserves contextual continuity across segment boundaries while keeping each input within the encoder’s length limit. Every segment is passed independently through DNABERT-2 to obtain token-level contextual embeddings, which are combined by mean pooling over the sequence-length dimension to yield one fixed-length vector per segment. The segment vectors originating from the same contig are then averaged to form a single contig-level representation Econtig,iE_{\text{contig},i}, and the contig-level vectors are in turn aggregated into one isolate-level vector through a length-aware weighted average in which longer contigs, being more information-rich, contribute proportionally more to the final representation. The isolate embedding EisolateE_{\text{isolate}} is computed as:

Eisolate=∑i=1nLi∑j=1nLj⋅Econtig,iE_{\text{isolate}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{L_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}L_{j}}\cdot E_{\text{contig},i} (1)

where nn is the number of contigs in the isolate, LiL_{i} is the length of the ii-th contig, and Econtig,iE_{\text{contig},i} is its representation. The result is a 768-dimensional vector that summarizes the genomic characteristics of the isolate and serves as the conditioning input to the GAN framework.

4.2 GAN-based Genome-to-Image Translation

Let 𝐱∈[−1,1]3×64×64\mathbf{x}\in[-1,1]^{3\times 64\times 64} denote a colony microscopy image of a bacterial isolate, and let 𝐜\mathbf{c} denote the set of biological conditioning signals associated with that image. The objective of the generative model is to learn a generator GG and a critic DD such that the model distribution pG​(𝐱∣𝐜)p_{G}(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c}) approximates the true data distribution pdata​(𝐱∣𝐜)p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{c}).

The conditioning context 𝐜\mathbf{c} differs between the two training phases.

In Phase 1, 𝐜=(E,y)\mathbf{c}=(E,y) consists of two signals: the isolate embedding E∈ℝ768E\in\mathbb{R}^{768} derived from DNABERT-2 (Section 4.1), which encodes the genomic identity of the bacterial strain; and the antibiotic treatment label y∈{0,…,3}y\in\{0,\ldots,3\}, corresponding to the four treatment conditions in the dataset: no drug, azithromycin (AZI), tetracycline (TE), and ciprofloxacin (CIP). All four conditions are included to expose the model to the full range of colony morphology across treatment states. The Phase 1 objective is to learn pG​(𝐱∣E,y)p_{G}(\mathbf{x}\mid E,y).

In Phase 2, 𝐜=(E,y,r)\mathbf{c}=(E,y,r) extends the Phase 1 conditioning with a third signal: the antimicrobial resistance status r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\}, where r=0r=0 denotes susceptibility and r=1r=1 denotes resistance of the isolate to the applied drug. Since resistance status is clinically meaningful only in the presence of a specific antibiotic, images collected under the no-drug condition are excluded, reducing the drug label space to y∈{0,1,2}y\in\{0,1,2\} (AZI, TE, CIP). The Phase 2 objective is to learn pG​(𝐱∣E,y,r)p_{G}(\mathbf{x}\mid E,y,r).

4.2.1 Generator Architecture

Figure 3 illustrates the overall generator architecture, showing the three functional components: the multi-modal conditioning fusion module, the pretrained CNN backbone encoder, and the FiLM-conditioned U-Net decoder. The generator operates in two modes during training: pure generation mode synthesizes images from noise 𝐳\mathbf{z} without skip connections and is used for the adversarial objective; reconstruction mode encodes a real image through the backbone to extract skip features before decoding, and is used for the reconstruction objective.

Multi-modal conditioning fusion.

In Phase 1, three independent branches encode the input signals into a shared conditioning representation. The noise branch projects 𝐳∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈100)\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{100}) through a two-layer MLP with ReLU, LayerNorm, and Dropout (p=0.2p{=}0.2) to 𝐟z∈ℝ512\mathbf{f}_{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{512}. The DNA branch maps EE to 𝐟E∈ℝ512\mathbf{f}_{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{512} via a three-layer MLP with ReLU, LayerNorm, and Dropout (p=0.2p{=}0.2). The antibiotic branch looks up a learnable embedding 𝐞y∈ℝ128\mathbf{e}_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{128} for label yy and projects it to 𝐟y∈ℝ256\mathbf{f}_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{256} through a two-layer MLP with ReLU and LayerNorm. The three outputs are concatenated to form 𝐟=[𝐟z​‖𝐟E‖​𝐟y]∈ℝ1280\mathbf{f}=[\,\mathbf{f}_{z}\;\|\;\mathbf{f}_{E}\;\|\;\mathbf{f}_{y}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{1280}.

In Phase 2, a fourth resistance branch is added to the fusion module: a learnable embedding 𝐞r∈ℝ64\mathbf{e}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{64} for the resistance label rr is projected to 𝐟r∈ℝ128\mathbf{f}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{128} through a two-layer MLP with ReLU and LayerNorm, and concatenated with the other branches, extending the fused vector to:

𝐟=[𝐟z∥𝐟E∥𝐟y∥𝐟r]∈ℝ1408.\mathbf{f}=[\,\mathbf{f}_{z}\;\|\;\mathbf{f}_{E}\;\|\;\mathbf{f}_{y}\;\|\;\mathbf{f}_{r}\,]\in\mathbb{R}^{1408}. (2)

In both phases, a self-gating mechanism scales 𝐟\mathbf{f} element-wise by a learned attention mask:

𝐟~=𝐟⊙σ⁡(𝐖2​tanh⁡(𝐖1​𝐟+𝐛1)+𝐛2),\tilde{\mathbf{f}}=\mathbf{f}\odot\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{2}\,\tanh\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{1}\,\mathbf{f}+\mathbf{b}_{1}\right)+\mathbf{b}_{2}\right), (3)

where 𝐖1,𝐖2∈ℝd×d\mathbf{W}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are learned weight matrices with corresponding bias vectors 𝐛1,𝐛2∈ℝd,d=1280\mathbf{b}_{1},\mathbf{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},d=1280 in Phase 1 and d=1408d=1408 in Phase 2, and σ\sigma is the sigmoid function. The gated representation 𝐟~\tilde{\mathbf{f}} is then projected to 𝐜~∈ℝ2048\tilde{\mathbf{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2048} through a two-layer MLP with ReLU, LayerNorm, and Dropout (p=0.2p{=}0.2).Within the decoder, 𝐜~\tilde{\mathbf{c}} serves exclusively as the source of the spatial seed 𝐬\mathbf{s} in pure generation mode, while 𝐟~\tilde{\mathbf{f}} provides the conditioning signal for all FiLM layers.

Pretrained CNN backbone encoder.

The generator employs a pretrained CNN backbone to extract hierarchical multi-scale visual features from the input image. The backbone is modular and interchangeable; in Phase 1, seven pretrained architectures are evaluated under identical conditions: VGG-16 Simonyan and Zisserman (2014), ResNet-101 He et al. (2016), EfficientNet-B0 Tan and Le (2019), DenseNet-121 Huang et al. (2017), InceptionNet-V1 Szegedy et al. (2015), ConvNeXt-Tiny Liu et al. (2022), and MobileNetV2 Sandler et al. (2018), all initialised with ImageNet-pretrained weights. The selection criterion and results of this ablation are reported in Section 5.1. In Phase 2, the backbone is fixed to ConvNeXt-Tiny, the best-performing variant identified in Phase 1.

Regardless of backbone choice, feature maps are extracted at four spatial downsampling scales. For the ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone, the output channels are [96,192,384,768][96,192,384,768] at spatial resolutions 16×1616{\times}16, 8×88{\times}8, 4×44{\times}4, and 2×22{\times}2 respectively (for a 64×6464{\times}64 input). The deepest feature map is further processed by a 3×33{\times}3 convolution to 512 channels, followed by BatchNorm, ReLU, a residual block, and a self-attention layer Zhang et al. (2019), yielding the spatial seed 𝐬∈ℝ512×2×2\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{512\times 2\times 2}. In pure generation mode, the spatial seed is obtained from 𝐜~\tilde{\mathbf{c}} via a learned linear projection: 𝐬=reshape⁡(𝐖s​𝐜~)\mathbf{s}=\mathrm{reshape}(\mathbf{W}_{s}\,\tilde{\mathbf{c}}), 𝐖s:ℝ2048→ℝ2048\mathbf{W}_{s}:\mathbb{R}^{2048}\to\mathbb{R}^{2048}.

FiLM-conditioned U-Net decoder.

The decoder upsamples 𝐬\mathbf{s} through five transposed convolution blocks to a 64×6464{\times}64 feature map. Each block contains a transposed convolution (4×44{\times}4 kernel, stride 2, padding 1), BatchNorm, ReLU, and a residual block. The block at the 8×88{\times}8 scale additionally contains a self-attention layer. In reconstruction mode, skip connections from the backbone are concatenated with decoder activations at matching scales and merged via 1×11{\times}1 pointwise convolution; bilinear interpolation is applied when spatial dimensions do not match. Conditioning is injected at the first four decoder stages (4×4, 8×8, 16×16, and 32×32) via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) Perez et al. (2018):

𝐡~=(1+𝜸)⊙𝐡+𝜷,\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=(1+\bm{\gamma})\odot\mathbf{h}+\bm{\beta}, (4)

where (𝜸,𝜷)∈ℝC(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta})\in\mathbb{R}^{C} are the modulation parameters and CC is the number of channels at that scale. Both parameters are jointly predicted from 𝐟~\tilde{\mathbf{f}} by a two-layer MLP with ReLU activation that projects 𝐟~\tilde{\mathbf{f}} to ℝ2​C\mathbb{R}^{2C}, whose output is split evenly into 𝜸\bm{\gamma} and 𝜷\bm{\beta}. The output layer applies two 3×33{\times}3 convolutions (32→16→332{\to}16{\to}3 channels) with ReLU and Tanh, producing 𝐱^∈[−1,1]3×64×64\hat{\mathbf{x}}\in[-1,1]^{3\times 64\times 64}.

4.2.2 Critic Architecture

The Critic DD is a multi-modal critic that jointly evaluates an image against the full conditioning context 𝐜\mathbf{c}, thereby penalising outputs that are either visually unrealistic or inconsistent with their associated biological context. The design rationale and the training instabilities that motivated this choice are discussed in Section 4.2.3. Figure 4 illustrates the critic architecture, in which image features and conditioning signals are processed in parallel branches before being concatenated and passed through a shared MLP to produce a single Wasserstein score.

The critic backbone processes the input image as a separate instance from the generator backbone and returns the deepest feature map, which is flattened and projected to ℝ512\mathbb{R}^{512} via a linear layer with LeakyReLU (α=0.2\alpha{=}0.2) and Dropout (p=0.4p{=}0.4).

In Phase 1, two conditioning branches process the non-image inputs in parallel alongside the image features: the DNA branch maps EE to ℝ256\mathbb{R}^{256} via a two-layer MLP with LeakyReLU and Dropout (p=0.3p{=}0.3); and the antibiotic branch encodes yy as a KK-dimensional one-hot vector and projects it to ℝ64\mathbb{R}^{64} with LeakyReLU and Dropout (p=0.2p{=}0.2). The three representations are concatenated to 832832 dimensions and passed through a three-layer MLP critic head with LeakyReLU and Dropout (p=0.5p{=}0.5) to produce a single real-valued Wasserstein score without sigmoid activation.

In Phase 2, a third resistance branch is added: the resistance status rr is encoded as a two-dimensional one-hot vector and projected to ℝ32\mathbb{R}^{32} with LeakyReLU and Dropout (p=0.2p{=}0.2), extending the concatenated representation to 864864 dimensions.

Backbone selection for the critic.

Computing the gradient penalty under WGAN-GP requires extracting per-sample gradients from interpolated inputs (Section 4.2.3). Batch Normalization (BN) computes mean and variance statistics across the entire mini-batch, introducing inter-sample information leakage that corrupts the independent per-sample gradient signal required by the penalty term. Any backbone containing BN layers is therefore mathematically incompatible with gradient penalty computation and cannot be used inside the critic.

Among the seven backbone architectures evaluated in Phase 1, Batch Normalization layers are present in ResNet-101, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121, InceptionNet-V1, and MobileNetV2. For these five cases, the critic backbone is substituted with ConvNeXt-Tiny, which replaces Batch Normalization with Layer Normalization and is therefore compatible with per-sample gradient computation. For the remaining two backbones (ConvNeXt-Tiny and VGG-16) the critic uses the same backbone as the generator, as neither architecture contains Batch Normalization. This substitution policy ensures gradient penalty validity across all ablation experiments while keeping the critic capacity as consistent as possible with the generator.

4.2.3 Training Objectives

Both phases adopt the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) Gulrajani et al. (2017) as the adversarial training framework. WGAN-GP optimizes the Wasserstein-1 distance between the real and generated distributions, enforcing a Lipschitz constraint on the critic via a gradient penalty on interpolated samples rather than weight clipping. We select WGAN-GP over the original GAN formulation Goodfellow et al. (2014) for three reasons specific to our setting. First, training stability is critical when the conditioning space is high-dimensional: the 768-dimensional genomic embedding combined with discrete treatment and resistance labels creates a complex conditional distribution that is prone to mode collapse and vanishing gradients under a standard GAN critic. Second, the Wasserstein distance provides a smoother and more informative gradient signal than the Jensen–Shannon divergence, which is particularly beneficial in the early stages of training when the generator has not yet learned to produce recognizable colony structure and the real and generated distributions have limited overlap. Finally, the gradient penalty enforces the Lipschitz constraint without restricting the critic architecture, allowing us to use a pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone inside the critic without weight clipping interference.

Training instabilities and iterative solutions.

Two failure modes were encountered during preliminary training and resolved through successive interventions, motivating the final objective design.

In the first failure mode, training with only the adversarial objective caused the generator to consistently produce entirely black images — a degenerate solution that satisfies the Wasserstein distance in early training before the critic has learned to provide informative gradients. A pixel-level reconstruction loss was introduced to resolve this, anchoring the generator output to real colony appearance from the first training epoch.

In the second failure mode, adding the reconstruction loss eliminated the all-black output but introduced conditioning-space mode collapse: the generator converged to a single “average colony” image regardless of isolate identity or antibiotic condition, satisfying reconstruction error while ignoring all conditioning signals. This was resolved by adopting a conditional WGAN-GP formulation in which the critic receives the full conditioning context 𝐜\mathbf{c} alongside the image, forcing the critic to jointly evaluate realism and conditioning consistency and thereby driving inter-class diversity.

Adversarial loss.

Training follows the WGAN-GP protocol Gulrajani et al. (2017) with ncritic=5n_{\text{critic}}=5 critic updates per generator step. The critic objective is:

ℒD=−𝔼𝐱∼pdata​(x|c)​[D⁡(𝐱,𝐜)]+𝔼𝐳∼pz,c​[D⁡(G⁡(𝐳,𝐜),𝐜)]+λGP​ℒGP,\mathcal{L}_{D}=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{\text{data}(x|c)}}\bigl[D(\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{c})\bigr]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim p_{z},c}\bigl[D(G(\mathbf{z},\,\mathbf{c}),\,\mathbf{c})\bigr]+\lambda_{\text{GP}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{GP}}, (5)

where the gradient penalty is computed on interpolated samples 𝐱^=α​𝐱+(1−α)​G​(𝐳,𝐜)\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\alpha\,\mathbf{x}+(1{-}\alpha)\,G(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{c}), α∼𝒰⁡[0,1]\alpha\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1]:

ℒGP=𝔼𝐱^,c​[(‖∇𝐱^D​(𝐱^,𝐜)‖2−1)2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{GP}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\hat{\mathbf{x}},c}}\!\left[\Bigl(\bigl\|\nabla_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}D(\hat{\mathbf{x}},\,\mathbf{c})\bigr\|_{2}-1\Bigr)^{\!2}\right], (6)

with λGP=10\lambda_{\text{GP}}=10.

Reconstruction loss.

For each real training image 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the generator backbone encodes 𝐱\mathbf{x} to extract multi-scale skip features, and the decoder reconstructs 𝐱\mathbf{x} under the correct conditioning:

ℒrecon=‖Grecon​(𝐱,𝐜)−𝐱‖1,\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}=\bigl\|G_{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{x}\bigr\|_{1}, (7)

where GreconG_{\text{recon}} denotes the encode-then-decode path.

Total generator objective.
ℒG=−𝔼𝐳​[D⁡(G⁡(𝐳,𝐜),𝐜)]+λrecon​ℒrecon,\mathcal{L}_{G}=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}}\!\bigl[D(G(\mathbf{z},\,\mathbf{c}),\,\mathbf{c})\bigr]+\lambda_{\text{recon}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}, (8)

with λrecon=100\lambda_{\text{recon}}=100. The high reconstruction weight ensures pixel-level stability during early training while the conditional critic drives inter-class diversity as training progresses. For each training step, the critic is updated ncritic=5n_{\text{critic}}=5 times using real samples and generated samples from the pure generation path. The generator is then updated once using a combined objective consisting of adversarial loss from the pure generation path and reconstruction loss from the reconstruction path. The reconstruction path is used only during training to stabilize optimization and is disabled at validation and test time, where only the pure generation path is used for image synthesis.

4.2.4 Implementation Details

Both the generator and critic are optimized using Adam Kingma and Ba (2015) with β1=0\beta_{1}=0, β2=0.9\beta_{2}=0.9, and learning rate 10−410^{-4} for both networks in both phases. Training runs for a maximum of 50 epochs with batch size 512, latent dimension dz=100d_{z}=100, and image resolution 64×6464{\times}64.

Image preprocessing.

Prior to model input, each image undergoes adaptive contrast enhancement. The mean pixel intensity I¯\bar{I} is computed over the grayscale channel and a contrast scale factor is derived as:

α=54​max⁡(I¯,ϵ)+ϵ+1,\alpha=\frac{5}{4\,\max(\bar{I},\,\epsilon)+\epsilon}+1, (9)

where ϵ=10−2\epsilon=10^{-2} prevents division by zero. Darker images (lower I¯\bar{I}) receive stronger enhancement; brighter images are adjusted more conservatively. The enhanced image is converted to RGB and normalised to [−1,1][-1,1] per channel with mean (0.5,0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5,0.5) and standard deviation (0.5,0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5,0.5).

Checkpoint selection in Phase 1.

During the backbone ablation study, the best checkpoint for each backbone variant is selected using the mean per-class FID on the validation set. FID is evaluated independently for each (isolate, antibiotic) class pair at the end of every epoch; the checkpoint achieving the lowest average across all valid classes (those with at least 10 validation samples) is retained as the representative of that backbone. Per-class averaging is preferred over a global FID because the dataset is class-imbalanced: a global metric is dominated by high-frequency classes and fails to penalise poor performance on rarer isolate–drug combinations.

Checkpoint selection in Phase 2.

The final model (ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone with resistance conditioning) employs a min-max FID checkpoint selection strategy. At each epoch, the maximum per-class FID across all valid classes is computed:

FIDmax=maxk∈𝒞⁡FIDk,\text{FID}_{\max}=\max_{k\in\mathcal{C}}\,\text{FID}_{k}, (10)

and a checkpoint is saved whenever FIDmax\text{FID}_{\max} improves. This strategy focuses training on the worst-performing class at each epoch rather than on the class average, ensuring that no (isolate, antibiotic) combination is neglected - a property essential for the downstream resistance classification task, which must generalise across all class combinations. Early stopping monitors FIDmax\text{FID}_{\max} as the tracked metric.

5 Experimental Results

Image quality is evaluated by two widely adopted metrics for generative models: the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), introduced by Heusel et al. in 2017 Heusel et al. (2017), and the Kernel Inception Distance (KID), proposed by Bińkowski et al. in 2018 Bińkowski et al. (2018). Both metrics are computed from feature representations extracted from the final average pooling layer of a pre-trained Inception-v3 network.

FID assumes that the extracted features follow multivariate Gaussian distributions and computes the Fréchet distance between the real and generated feature distributions using their means and covariance matrices:

FID​(R,G)=|μR−μG|22+Tr​(ΣR+ΣG−2​ΣR​ΣG)\text{FID}(R,G)=|\mu_{R}-\mu_{G}|^{2}_{2}+\text{Tr}\left(\Sigma_{R}+\Sigma_{G}-2\sqrt{\Sigma_{R}\Sigma_{G}}\right)

where μR\mu_{R} and μG\mu_{G} denote the feature means, and ΣR\Sigma_{R} and ΣG\Sigma_{G} denote the corresponding covariance matrices of the real and generated distributions.

In contrast, KID does not rely on Gaussian assumptions and instead computes the squared Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the two feature distributions:

KID​(R,G)=M​M​D2=𝔼x,x′∼R​[k⁡(x,x′)]+𝔼y,y′∼G​[k⁡(y,y′)]−2​𝔼x∼R,y∼G​[k⁡(x,y)]\text{KID}(R,G)=MMD^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim R}[k(x,x^{\prime})]+\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim G}[k(y,y^{\prime})]-2\mathbb{E}_{x\sim R,y\sim G}[k(x,y)]

where 𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes expectation and k⁡(x,y)=(1d​x⊤​y+1)3k(x,y)=(\frac{1}{d}x^{\top}y+1)^{3} is the polynomial kernel function, with dd representing the feature dimension.

Unlike FID’s reliance on mean and covariance, KID is sensitive to higher-order distributional differences through its kernel formulation and provides an unbiased estimator even for relatively small sample sizes. Lower FID/KID scores indicate better similarity between synthetic and real distributions.

Additionally, we report the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) Wang et al. (2004) to assess the perceptual similarity between generated and real bacterial cells. Unlike FID and KID, which evaluate distribution-level similarity, SSIM measures image-level similarity based on luminance, contrast, and structural information:

SSIM​(x,y)=[l⁡(x,y)]α⋅[c⁡(x,y)]β⋅[s⁡(x,y)]γ\text{SSIM}(x,y)=[l(x,y)]^{\alpha}\cdot[c(x,y)]^{\beta}\cdot[s(x,y)]^{\gamma} where:

l⁡(x,y)=2​μx​μy+C1μx2+μy2+C1,c⁡(x,y)=2​σx​σy+C2σx2+σy2+C2,s⁡(x,y)=σx​y+C3σx​σy+C3l(x,y)=\frac{2\mu_{x}\mu_{y}+C_{1}}{\mu_{x}^{2}+\mu_{y}^{2}+C_{1}},\quad c(x,y)=\frac{2\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}+C_{2}}{\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{y}^{2}+C_{2}},\quad s(x,y)=\frac{\sigma_{xy}+C_{3}}{\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}+C_{3}}

For evaluation, each generated image is compared with all real images belonging to the same isolate-antibiotic class. The SSIM score of a generated image is defined as the average SSIM across these pairwise comparisons. The final SSIM reported for a model is obtained by averaging over all generated images. Higher SSIM values indicate that generated cells exhibit luminance, contrast, and structural characteristics similar to those observed in real bacterial cells. However, because SSIM measures pairwise similarity between images, it does not directly assess distributional diversity and is therefore reported alongside FID and KID.

5.1 Backbone Comparison Results

The performance of the proposed cWGAN-GP architecture with seven different pretrained CNN backbones is assessed by the evaluation metrics described above. These backbones serve as the visual feature extractor within the generator, providing the multi-scale image representations from which the decoder synthesizes colony images; the critic backbone follows the substitution policy described in Section 4.2.2. The evaluated architectures include ConvNeXt-Tiny, DenseNet121, MobileNet-V2, ResNet101, EfficientNet-B0, VGG-16, and InceptionNet-V1.

The quantitative results are summarized in Table 4. According to the distribution-based metrics, ConvNeXt-Tiny achieved the lowest FID (80.88) and KID (0.026) scores among all evaluated backbones, indicating the closest alignment between the generated and real image distributions. DenseNet121 and MobileNet-V2 produced similarly competitive results, whereas ResNet101 and EfficientNet-B0 exhibited moderately higher FID and KID values. In contrast, VGG-16 and InceptionNet-V1 yielded substantially worse scores, suggesting that these architectures were less effective as feature extractors within the proposed cWGAN-GP framework. Notably, FID and KID exhibited a consistent ranking across all backbones, indicating strong agreement between the two distribution-based evaluation metrics.

In terms of image-level similarity, EfficientNet-B0 and InceptionNet-V1 achieved the highest average SSIM scores (0.809), and the remaining backbones produced comparable SSIM values. SSIM remained relatively stable (0.782–0.809), suggesting that most generated images preserved similar local structural characteristics of real bacterial microscopy images, despite large differences in distributional realism (as FID and KID varied substantially across backbones).

However, the discrepancy between SSIM and the distribution-based metrics is particularly evident for EfficientNet-B0 and InceptionNet-V1, which achieved among the highest SSIM scores despite exhibiting substantially worse FID and KID values. This observation highlights an important limitation of SSIM: although it measures perceptual similarity between individual image pairs, it does not directly evaluate distributional realism or sample diversity. Consequently, SSIM is reported as a complementary reference metric, whereas FID and KID are considered the primary criteria for backbone selection.

Based on the consistently superior FID and KID performance, ConvNeXt-Tiny was selected as the generator backbone for all subsequent experiments. Figure 5 shows representative real and synthetic cells produced by this configuration under each antibiotic.

5.2 Downstream Classification Performance

To evaluate the practical utility of our generative model, we examine whether synthetic images from our cWGAN-GP can improve classification performance when real training data is scarce. Three independent binary classification tasks are defined, one per antibiotic (AZI, TE, CIP), predicting resistant (R) vs. susceptible (S) phenotypes for each drug separately. All classifiers use a fully fine-tuned ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone with a lightweight MLP head. Each drug-specific classifier is tuned independently over class-weighted cross-entropy, dropout rate, backbone and head learning rates, and input noise intensity, with early stopping on the validation set.

All splits are performed at the microscopy-image level, so that cell images originating from the same microscopy image never appear in more than one split. We consider two protocols. (i) Isolate-agnostic splitting: images from all isolates are pooled and partitioned randomly, so the same isolate may appear in all three splits. (ii) Isolate-aware splitting: 80% of the 22 isolates are assigned to the training pool and the remaining isolates form the test set; the validation set is drawn from 25% of the training-pool images, so a training isolate may contribute to both training and validation but never to testing. This protocol measures generalization to unseen isolates.

To simulate a low-data regime, we reduce the real training cells to 25% per image. This ratio was selected after a preliminary study at 100%, 50% and 25% confirmed that performance degrades proportionally, leaving sufficient headroom for augmentation to produce a measurable effect. The number of images remains unchanged; only the cell count per image is reduced. This reduced dataset serves as the baseline training set. For augmentation, we train a cWGAN-GP variant extended with an additional conditioning branch for resistance/susceptibility labels. Synthetic cells conditioned on antibiotic type and resistance status are added to the baseline training set. The number of synthetic cells is set to 50% of the number of real cells retained in the baseline training set, forming the GAN-augmented training set. Final evaluation for both conditions is performed exclusively on the held-out real test set, containing no synthetic samples, so that reported metrics reflect generalization to real microscopy images.

Classifier performance is evaluated using several standard metrics, including Precision, Recall, F1-Score, Accuracy, and AUC. These metrics provide complementary perspectives on classification performance by measuring prediction correctness, class sensitivity, and the balance between precision and recall. The corresponding definitions are given below:

Accuracy =TP+TNTP+FP+TN+FN\displaystyle=\frac{\text{TP}+\text{TN}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}+\text{TN}+\text{FN}} (11)
Precision =TPTP+FP\displaystyle=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}} (12)
Recall =TPTP+FN\displaystyle=\frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP}+\text{FN}} (13)
F1-Score =2×Precision×RecallPrecision+Recall\displaystyle=2\times\frac{\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}} (14)

The complete image generation, training, and evaluation pipeline was repeated using five different random seeds to assess performance. For each seed, the baseline and GAN-augmented models were trained and evaluated using identical data splits, enabling paired statistical comparisons.

Table 5 and Figure 6 report the results when isolates may be shared across splits. Baseline performance is already high (AUC ≥0.9\geq 0.9 for all antibiotics) and stable across seeds. GAN augmentation improved most mean scores, with significant gains in four metrics for AZI, four for TE, and two for CIP. Recall (R) increased significantly for all three antibiotics, by 0.0830.083, 0.2100.210, and 0.1000.100 for AZI (p=0.012p=0.012), TE (p=0.0005p=0.0005), and CIP (p=0.031p=0.031), respectively. Accuracy improved by 0.0470.047 for AZI (p=0.044p=0.044) and 0.0850.085 for TE (p=0.004p=0.004), and by 0.0490.049 for CIP, which was not significant (p=0.065p=0.065). F1-Score (R) improved significantly for AZI and TE (0.0440.044 and 0.1190.119), and Precision (S) for all three antibiotics (0.0650.065, 0.1230.123 and 0.1010.101).

These gains come with a trade-off. Precision (R) decreased for AZI (0.0230.023) and TE (0.0620.062), and Recall (S) decreased for AZI (0.0670.067) and TE (0.1080.108), while AUC remained essentially unchanged (differences ≤0.006\leq 0.006; p>0.38p>0.38 where tested). This suggests that the augmented models operate at a different point on a similar ROC curve, with a decision boundary shifted toward higher sensitivity for the resistant class: resistance is flagged more readily, at the cost of occasionally misclassifying susceptible isolates. In clinical practice this trade-off may be acceptable, as missing a resistant case (false susceptibility) generally has more severe consequences than a false resistance call.

Table 6 and Figure 7 report the results when test isolates are never seen during training. This is the more demanding setting: absolute performance is markedly lower and more variable across seeds than under isolate-agnostic splitting. Baseline accuracy is only 0.5560.556 (AZI), 0.3210.321 (TE) and 0.7500.750 (CIP). The large standard deviations (e.g., Recall (S) of 0.550±0.5120.550\pm 0.512 for TE) are consistent with the small number of test isolates, where a change in the prediction for a single image shifts the metrics substantially.

Despite this difficulty, GAN augmentation yielded higher mean Accuracy for all three antibiotics (0.0510.051 for AZI, 0.0550.055 for TE, and 0.0360.036 for CIP), although none of these differences reached significance. Statistically significant improvements (p<0.05p<0.05) were found in two metrics for AZI (Recall (R), F1-Score (R)), one for TE (Recall (R)), and four for CIP (Precision (R), Recall (S), F1-Score (S), AUC).

For AZI and TE, the baseline detects few resistant isolates (Recall (R) of 0.4500.450 and 0.2480.248), and augmentation significantly raises this recall (to 0.550, p=0.038p=0.038 for AZI, and to 0.3200.320, p=0.044p=0.044 for TE). This improvement is potentially clinically relevant because a resistant isolate misclassified as susceptible could lead to inappropriate antibiotic treatment. For CIP, the baseline almost always predicts resistant (Recall (R) =0.960=0.960) but rarely identifies susceptible isolates (Recall (S) =0.225=0.225), and augmentation mainly improves the susceptible class (Recall (S): from 0.2250.225 to 0.3500.350; p=0.045p=0.045, F1-Score (S): from 0.3140.314 to 0.4690.469, p=0.041p=0.041), while keeping Recall (R) unchanged at 0.9600.960. CIP is the only antibiotic for which the threshold-independent AUC improved significantly (from 0.7580.758 to 0.8060.806, p=0.023p=0.023).

In other words, augmentation tends to improve the class the baseline handles worst. The one visible cost is for AZI, where Precision (R) and Recall (S) decrease slightly (0.0250.025 and 0.0860.086, not significant).

5.3 Discussion

Two findings are consistent across both strategies. First, GAN augmentation significantly improved Recall (R) for AZI and TE under both strategies, and for CIP under the isolate-agnostic strategy, where the baseline had more room to improve (from 0.8730.873 to 0.9730.973, p=0.031p=0.031). Under isolate-aware splitting, CIP Recall (R) was already high at baseline (0.9600.960) and remained unchanged. Second, the gains are concentrated in the class that the baseline predicts least reliably.

Under isolate-agnostic splitting, improvements are larger and more uniform, but test isolates also appear in training, so the classifier may exploit isolate-specific appearance rather than resistance-related morphology. Under isolate-aware splitting, performance drops sharply and improvements are smaller and drug-dependent.

Overall, GAN-based augmentation consistently improves the detection of resistant isolates, which is the clinically most important outcome, at the cost of a modest reduction in resistant-class precision and susceptible-class recall for some antibiotics.

There are still several limitations. First, the augmentation ratio is fixed at 50% of the baseline training set; whether smaller (e.g., 25%) or larger (e.g., 100%) ratios would yield better or worse results remains untested. Second, the GAN was trained on the same dataset as the classifiers, sharing the same image-level train/validation/test splits. While cell-level separation ensures no direct leakage of test samples into GAN training, the generative model has implicitly learned the statistical distribution of the full training pool, which may inflate the apparent benefit of augmentation. Future work should validate this augmentation strategy on a held-out external dataset to provide a more unbiased estimate of its practical utility.

6 Conclusion and Future Works

We studied whether the morphology of an E. coli isolate under antibiotic challenge can be synthesized from its genome, and formulated the task as conditional image generation driven by a genomic foundation-model embedding. The framework combines a genomic encoding pipeline, which reduces the raw paired-end reads of an isolate to one 768-dimensional vector through a segment–contig–isolate hierarchy with length-aware aggregation, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty that generates colony images from that embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance status. Reaching a usable model required more than the adversarial objective alone: a pixel-level reconstruction term was needed to escape the degenerate all-black solution, and conditioning the critic on the full biological context was needed to escape the subsequent collapse onto a single average colony.

Among seven ImageNet-pretrained backbones evaluated inside the generator under identical conditions, ConvNeXt-Tiny gave the best distributional agreement with real images (FID 80.88, KID 0.026), while SSIM stayed within a narrow band (0.782–0.809) across all backbones and ranked EfficientNet-B0 and InceptionNet-V1 highly despite their much worse FID and KID. We therefore treat SSIM as a complementary reference rather than a selection criterion in this setting.

The extrinsic evaluation is the more informative one. Adding resistance-conditioned synthetic cells to a training set reduced to 25% of its real cells improved resistant-class recall significantly for all three antibiotics when isolates were shared across splits (by 0.083 for AZI, 0.210 for TE, and 0.100 for CIP), and accuracy rose for every antibiotic under both splitting protocols. Under the stricter protocol, in which no test isolate is seen during training, absolute performance fell sharply and the gains became smaller and drug-dependent, with significant improvements in resistant-class recall for AZI and TE and in the susceptible-class metrics and AUC for CIP. Across both protocols the improvement concentrated in whichever class the baseline handled worst, and it came with a modest loss of resistant-class precision and susceptible-class recall for some drugs. For antimicrobial susceptibility testing that trade-off is usually the preferable direction, since a resistant isolate reported as susceptible carries a heavier clinical cost than the converse, but the drop in the isolate-aware setting shows that generalization to unseen isolates remains the binding constraint rather than image fidelity.

Several limitations bound these conclusions and set the agenda for further work. The dataset is a single species represented by 22 isolates from one specimen type, which is the main reason the isolate-aware results are both weak and high-variance; the large standard deviations there follow directly from the small number of test isolates. The generator and the classifiers were trained on the same dataset and the same image-level splits, so although cell-level separation prevents direct leakage of test samples into generator training, the generative model has seen the statistical distribution of the training pool and the apparent benefit of augmentation may be optimistic. Validation on an external, independently collected dataset is the single most important next step. The augmentation ratio was fixed at 50% of the retained real cells and was not swept, so the relationship between the amount of synthetic data and downstream performance is unknown. Images were generated at 64×6464{\times}64, which is sufficient for single-cell appearance but discards detail that higher-resolution synthesis might recover. Finally, the model is evaluated by what its samples do for a classifier and not by whether it has captured any specific resistance mechanism; relating the genomic embedding, or the generated morphology, to known resistance determinants would turn the framework from a data-augmentation tool into an interpretable one. Extending the panel beyond three antibiotics, enlarging the isolate cohort, and testing whether a single multi-drug conditional model outperforms the per-antibiotic classifiers used here are the natural continuations.
